anomaly_def.Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: Static mismatch between table structures / indexes and the workload forces queries into wide scans, non-covering lookups, and write hot-spots.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly: Engine parameters for memory, parallelism, checkpoints, and workers are mis-tuned relative to hardware capacity and workload mix.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly: Aggregate memory consumed by caches, work areas, and sessions exceeds the safe limit of the host, provoking OS-level pressure or OOM events.

When all three root causes coexist, the system exhibits a blended symptom set: 1) full-table or full-index scans initiated by poor schema design allocate large work-memory regions that grow unchecked because per-query and per-session limits are misconfigured; 2) the bloated memory footprint collides with an undersized or overgrown buffer pool, causing rapid eviction, cache-hit volatility, and emergency flushes; 3) checkpoint storms, log-write stalls, or background-worker backlogs appear while CPU and I/O devices remain paradoxically under-utilised; 4) the host shows paging, swap thrashing, or abrupt process termination, after which execution plans may oscillate unpredictably as statistics, caches, and parameter adaptive features struggle to stabilise.

Causal chain: Inefficient access paths produced by the schema/index mismatch dramatically increase the volume of rows read, sorted, and hashed. Because configuration parameters such as work-memory, temp-space thresholds, buffer-pool size, and parallel-worker caps are mis-set, each inflated operation reserves more memory than the host can realistically supply. The resulting ballooning of session and cache memory triggers the memory-allocation anomaly, pushing the operating system into paging and forcing the database to flush or evict useful buffers prematurely. These evictions, in turn, magnify the original design flaw by making every repeated table or index scan re-read pages from disk. Meanwhile, mis-tuned checkpoint and background housekeeping parameters amplify I/O bursts caused by the additional dirty pages. The feedback loop between bad access paths, misallocated resources, and systemic memory pressure leads to cascading slowdowns, erratic throughput, and, in extreme cases, service instability or crashes.

entry.official_definition: Specifies the timeout in seconds for attempts to acquire metadata locks.
entry.trigger_condition: A statement waits longer than lock_wait_timeout while attempting to acquire a metadata lock.
entry.workload_impact: The metadata lock acquisition fails and the statement does not proceed.
entry.default_behavior: Defined as a MySQL server system variable.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when a statement cannot obtain the required lock within the configured waiting window because another transaction or metadata operation is holding an incompatible lock.
entry.solution_guidance: Inspect blocking sessions, reduce conflicting transaction overlap, shorten transaction lifetime, and review lock scheduling and schema-change timing.
